concept.body: Decision guide for proportion problems: PARALLEL marks → Side-Splitter (AD/DB = AE/EC). ANGLE-BISECTOR mark → BD/DC = AB/AC. Matching ANGLE marks with proportional sides → similarity (AA / SAS~ / SSS~). Identify the configuration from the marks, then write a single proportion and cross-multiply.

explanationVariants: Parallel arrows point to the Side-Splitter Theorem.
A parallel mark means side-splitter proportions.

widget.prompt: Parallel arrows on a segment inside a triangle signal which theorem?

options.label: Side-Splitter Theorem
options.feedback: Parallel ⇒ side-splitter: the segment splits the sides proportionally.

options.label: Angle Bisector Theorem
options.feedback: That needs a bisected-angle mark, not parallel arrows.

options.label: Pythagorean Theorem
options.feedback: That needs a right angle. Parallel arrows ⇒ side-splitter.

options.label: Triangle Inequality
options.feedback: That's about side sums, unrelated to parallel marks. Parallel ⇒ side-splitter.

steps.body: Real figures stack these ideas. The skill is **spotting which proportion applies**: a parallel line means side-splitter; a shared angle with proportional sides means SAS~; an angle bisector means the bisector ratio. Read the figure's marks — parallel arrows, angle ticks — to choose the right tool, then set up ONE proportion.

widget.prompt: The arrows mark the inner segment as parallel to the base — that is what the marks are telling you. Slide the cut to the midpoint of AB and read both ratios the whole way.
widget.successFeedback: Both ratios read 1.00 — the cut has bisected AB and AC at once. The marks are the whole warrant: because the segment is parallel to the base, the two ratios are locked together, so cutting one side in half cuts the other in half too. That is the side-splitter theorem, and the midpoint case is the midsegment.
widget.lowFeedback: The cut is still above the midpoint — AD/DB is under 1.00. Keep sliding down, and watch the second ratio track the first the entire way rather than lagging behind it.
widget.highFeedback: Past the midpoint now — AD/DB has gone above 1.00. Ease back up. Notice that overshooting moved both readouts together; they have never once disagreed.

predict.prompt: A segment inside a triangle is marked parallel to the base. Sliding it up and down, the two side ratios AD/DB and AE/EC will…

options.label: Always match each other, at every position
Move independently — they measure different sides

predict.reveal: Always. Parallel to the base is the condition, and it holds at every height, so the two ratios are equal everywhere the cut can go — that is the side-splitter theorem, and the reason it can be used to solve for a missing length. The midpoint is not where the theorem starts working — it is just the position where both ratios happen to read 1.

explanationVariants: An angle-bisector mark triggers BD/DC = AB/AC; a parallel mark triggers the side-splitter. The figure's marks tell you which.
Match the mark to the theorem: bisector ⇒ adjacent-side ratio; parallel ⇒ side-splitter.

widget.prompt: A cevian from vertex A is marked as bisecting angle A. Which proportion applies?

options.label: BD/DC = AB/AC (Angle Bisector Theorem)
options.feedback: An angle-bisector mark triggers the bisector ratio: the opposite side splits as the adjacent sides do.

options.label: AD/DB = AE/EC (Side-Splitter)
options.feedback: That's for a PARALLEL line, not an angle bisector. The bisector gives BD/DC = AB/AC.

options.label: AB = AC (isosceles)
options.feedback: A bisector doesn't force equal sides. It gives the ratio BD/DC = AB/AC.

options.label: BD = DC (midpoint)
options.feedback: A bisector splits the opposite side PROPORTIONALLY to the adjacent sides, not into equal halves.

steps.body: When two similar triangles overlap, corresponding sides may be hard to pair. Anchor on the **equal angles** first — matching angle marks reveal which vertices correspond, and therefore which sides. Get the correspondence right, and the proportion writes itself.

widget.prompt: A parallel line gives △ADE ~ △ABC. AD = 6, AB = 15, and DE = 4. Find BC.

explanationVariants: Match equal angles first — they pin down which vertices (and sides) correspond before you write the ratio.
Equal angle marks reveal the correspondence, preventing mismatched sides.

widget.prompt: When two similar triangles overlap, what should you identify FIRST to pair corresponding sides?

options.label: The marked equal angles
options.feedback: Matching angles fix the correspondence of vertices, which then tells you which sides pair up.

options.label: The longest side lengths
options.feedback: Longest-to-longest can mislead in an overlap. Equal ANGLES reliably fix the correspondence.

options.label: The two triangle areas
options.feedback: Area doesn't reveal which parts correspond. Start from the equal angles.

options.label: The two triangle perimeters
options.feedback: Perimeter won't pair the sides. The equal angle marks do that.

steps.body: The master strategy for any proportion problem: (1) identify the configuration (parallel, bisector, or shared-angle similarity); (2) name the theorem; (3) write ONE proportion with corresponding parts aligned; (4) cross-multiply and solve. Same four steps, whatever the figure throws at you.

widget.prompt: Three parallel lines cut a transversal into 4 and 6, and a second transversal into x and 9. Find x.

commonErrors.feedback: 7 = 4 + 9 − 6 mixes pieces. Match ratios: 4/6 = x/9 → x = 4 × 9 ÷ 6 = 6.

hints: First use the side-splitter to find the missing piece on one side.
AD/DB = AE/EC with AD=6, DB=4, AE=9 finds EC.

widget.prompt: A parallel line splits the sides: AD = 6, DB = 4, AE = 9. Find EC.

takeaways: Read the marks: parallel ⇒ side-splitter, bisector ⇒ adjacent-side ratio, angles ⇒ similarity.
Anchor correspondence on equal angles before writing ratios.
Identify config → name theorem → one proportion → solve.
